title: The Chipotle of Indian Food Is No Longer a Punchline
excerpt: From Rasa's East Coast expansion to new openings in Columbus and Gastonia, Indian fast-casual dining is finally hitting its stride across America.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Rasa is expanding as a leading Indian fast-casual chain with five locations.
  • 49% of Americans have dined at an Indian restaurant, indicating growing popularity.
  • Indian cuisine is the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in the U.S.
  • New Indian restaurants are opening across the U.S., catering to diverse tastes.
  • The Indian fast-casual market could reach $1 billion in the next decade.

For years, the phrase "the Chipotle of Indian food" was the restaurant industry's favorite unfulfilled prophecy. Investors loved the pitch. Founders kept trying. And Indian fast-casual concepts kept stalling at three or four locations while Mexican, Mediterranean, and Asian bowls scaled to hundreds. That script is being rewritten — and this time, the momentum is real. ## Rasa Leads the Charge In Washington, D.C., childhood best friends Sahil Rahman and Rahul Vinod have quietly built Rasa into a five-unit fast-casual chain that is now primed for East Coast expansion. The brand recently secured a significant investment from Rellevant Partners, a female-founded growth equity firm, and added the former COO of Starbucks to its board of directors. The two grew up in restaurant families — their fathers, both first-generation Indian immigrants, jointly operate Bombay Bistro in Rockville, Maryland, and the upscale Indique in D.C. But where their fathers served traditional menus, Rahman and Vinod went a different direction. "We realized the biggest challenge was trying to eliminate barriers to entry for Indian cuisine," Rahman told Restaurant Business. "Instead of saag, it's sauteed spinach. It allows people to feel more welcome." The menu is built around customizable bowls with playfully named options — Tikka Chance on Me (chicken tikka with tomato-garlic sauce), Goa Your Own Way (spiced beef in coconut-ginger sauce), and Aloo Need Is Love. Rasa also serves Indian-spiced cocktails like a Masala Gin and Tonic and Spicy Mumbai Mule, and its vegan soft serve has become an unexpected hit. ## New Openings Everywhere The fast-casual trend is just one piece of a broader Indian restaurant boom across the country. In Columbus, Ohio, the Kondhare family is opening Bombay House Restaurant & Bar near Polaris this July — an upscale concept featuring pan-India cuisine spanning Mumbai street food, South Indian dosas, North Indian curries, and Indochinese dishes, along with handcrafted Indian-inspired cocktails. In Gastonia, North Carolina, Nawab Kabab Grill & Bar opened in June, bringing Indian buffet and table service to a city that its owner says was underserved. In Billerica, Massachusetts, chef and entrepreneur Palak Patel is preparing to open her first brick-and-mortar Indian restaurant after years of building a following through her catering and chai cart businesses. ## The Numbers Back It Up According to Datassential, 49 percent of American consumers have now eaten at an Indian restaurant, and Technomic reports that 52 percent of Americans have tried Indian food and liked it. Indian food is the second-fastest-growing global cuisine in America, and the US ethnic food market is valued at an estimated $24.5 billion. The supply chain has also matured. Tarka Indian Kitchen in Texas, which has expanded to nine locations, now works with a co-packer for its signature sauces and uses dough sheeters and rotary ovens instead of traditional tandoors — streamlining operations without sacrificing flavor. Curry Up Now in the Bay Area has simplified its prep to the point where, as founder Akash Kapoor notes, "there's not a single Indian cook in our fast-casual restaurants." ## Why This Matters for NRIs For the Indian diaspora, this wave is bittersweet validation. The cuisine their families served at home — complex, layered, deeply regional — is finally being taken seriously by American investors and consumers. But the versions that scale best are often simplified, Americanized, and stripped of the names their grandmothers used. Still, the net effect is positive. Every Rasa bowl that introduces an American college student to tamarind chili sauce, every Bombay House that serves vada pav in suburban Ohio, expands the market and makes room for the next generation of Indian restaurants — including the traditional ones. "Until very recently, I don't think the American palate was really open to Indian cuisine and culture in the way it is today," Rahman says. "What's been missing is a brand component, and a younger generation that's able to speak the language." ## What's Next Rasa is targeting additional East Coast locations, Tarka plans to expand beyond Texas to Atlanta, Denver, Nashville, and Arizona, and Curry Up Now is seeking drive-thru locations in North Carolina and along California's Highway 101. The Indian fast-casual segment, one industry leader predicts, could become a $1 billion category within the next decade.
